overview.headline: Louisiana Purchase doubled United States size westward

keyPoints.point: The United States bought vast land west of the Mississippi River for a low price per acre
keyPoints.quote: the United States purchased 828,000 square miles of land west of the Mississippi River for $15 million

keyPoints.point: Livingston and Monroe first sought New Orleans and the Floridas then accepted the larger Louisiana offer
keyPoints.quote: negotiators Robert Livingston and James Monroe were authorized to pay France up to $10 million

keyPoints.point: Jefferson held strict views of the Constitution yet moved ahead to occupy rich western lands
keyPoints.quote: President Thomas Jefferson was generally a strict interpreter of the Constitution

keyPoints.point: New western expansion exposed North South divisions over slavery and forced fragile compromises
keyPoints.quote: also exposed the sectional weaknesses between the North and South

keyTerms.gloss: first major cession of western land that began a series of expansions
keyTerms.quote: The Louisiana Purchase was the first major cession of land in a long series of expansions that span the 19th century.

keyTerms.gloss: agreement covering cession plus financial conventions for the transaction
keyTerms.quote: The Louisiana Purchase Agreement is made up of the Treaty of Cession and the two conventions regarding the financial aspects of the transaction.

keyTerms.gloss: states where slavery was not allowed, balanced against slave states
keyTerms.quote: the desire to maintain a balance between "free states" and "slave states" required a series of fragile compromises

keyTerms.gloss: peoples facing potential impact from purchase and loss of tribal lands
keyTerms.quote: In addition, the Louisiana Purchase ignored the potential impact on Native Americans.
